CHAPTER 5 · LEARNING AREA 5 · APRIL

Random events

How many packs of stickers do you have to buy until the album is full? How likely are you to win twice in a row on the wheel of fortune? How many possibilities does a combination lock have? Some questions you work out, others are quickest to try out a thousand times with the computer. You learn both: simulating random experiments and finding probabilities with a tree diagram, the path rules and clever counting.

14 LESSONS4 UNITS2 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • simulate random experiments with random numbers and interpret relative frequencies
  • represent multi-stage random experiments in a tree diagram and calculate with the path rules
  • tell apart drawing with and without replacement, use the complementary event
  • count possibilities with the counting principle and with $n!$

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Simulating random experiments

How many packs you need for the sticker album is hard to work out. But you can act it out: a dice replaces the packs. If you do this very often, you get a good estimate. This is called a simulation.

KEY POINT · FREQUENCY AND SIMULATION

In a random experiment several outcomes are possible; which one occurs cannot be predicted. An event groups outcomes together, for example “even number”.

Relative frequency = number of hits : number of trials

Law of large numbers: with very many trials the relative frequency settles down close to the probability.

Simulation: you replace the experiment by a simple random device, for example a dice, a coin or random numbers, and carry it out very often.

Random numbers: with the Ran# key of the calculator or in a spreadsheet with =RANDBETWEEN(1,6).

Laplace experiment: if all the outcomes are equally likely, $P(E) = \dfrac{\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\text{number of all outcomes}}$.

INTERACTIVE · THE LAW OF LARGE NUMBERS

Choose an experiment and carry it out 10, 100 and 1000 times. The relative frequency first fluctuates strongly and then settles down.

INTERACTIVE · WHEN IS THE ALBUM FULL?

Buy pack after pack or simulate a thousand albums at once.

EXAMPLE 1 · RELATIVE FREQUENCY

A dice is thrown 600 times, a six comes up 94 times. Compare the relative frequency with the probability.

$\tfrac{94}{600} \approx 0.157 = 15.7\%$. The probability is $\tfrac{1}{6} \approx 16.7\%$.

The values are close together; they are almost never exactly the same.

EXAMPLE 2 · PLANNING A SIMULATION

At a tombola, every fifth ticket wins. How often do you get at least two wins among 10 tickets? Plan a simulation.

Generate random numbers from 1 to 5, the 1 means a win. Every 10 numbers are one run. Count whether the 1 is there at least twice. Repeat this 1000 times.

The proportion of runs with at least two wins estimates the probability. It is about 62%.

EXERCISES

A coin is tossed 200 times, heads comes up 108 times. Work out the relative frequency and compare it with the probability.

$\tfrac{108}{200} = 0.54$. The probability is $0.5$. A difference of 4 percentage points is quite normal with 200 tosses.

How can you simulate with a dice: a) a coin toss   b) an event with the probability $\tfrac{1}{3}$   c) an event with the probability $\tfrac{1}{4}$?

a) even number = heads   b) 1 or 2 = hit   c) throw again on 5 or 6, otherwise the 1 is a hit (1 of 4 equally likely numbers).

A class repeated a random experiment many times: after 10 trials 4 hits, after 100 trials 31, after 1000 trials 334. Which probability do you suspect? Why are 10 trials not enough?

0.4, then 0.31, then 0.334: probably $\tfrac{1}{3}$. With 10 trials the relative frequency still fluctuates strongly.

For an album with 6 stickers a simulation gave 14.6 packs on average. It can be shown that on average $6 \cdot \left(1 + \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{3} + \tfrac{1}{4} + \tfrac{1}{5} + \tfrac{1}{6}\right)$ packs are needed. Work it out and compare.

The bracket gives 2.45, times 6 is 14.7. The simulation is very close to it.

1000 random points fall into a square with the side length 1. 786 of them lie in the quarter circle with the radius 1 around one corner. Estimate $\pi$ from this and explain why it works.

The quarter circle has the area $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$, the square the area 1. So the proportion of hits is about $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$: $\pi \approx 4 \cdot 0.786 = 3.144$.

TEST YOURSELF!

In 50 throws, a six comes up 9 times. What is the relative frequency?

$\tfrac{9}{50} = 0.18$

What does the law of large numbers say?

The dice has no memory. Only with very many trials does the relative frequency settle down.

Of 1000 random points in the square, 790 lie in the quarter circle. Which estimate of $\pi$ does that give?

$4 \cdot 0.79 = 3.16$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Tree diagram and path rules

A wheel of fortune is spun twice. At the first stage there are two or three outcomes, at the second the same ones again for each of them. A tree diagram shows all the paths clearly, and each branch is labelled with its probability.

KEY POINT · PATH RULES

A multi-stage random experiment consists of several random experiments one after the other. In the tree diagram, the branches that start at one point add up to 1.

Product rule (1st path rule): the probability of a path is the product of the probabilities along the path.

Sum rule (2nd path rule): the probability of an event is the sum of the probabilities of all the paths that belong to it.

Check: the probabilities of all the paths add up to 1.

Galton board: at each nail a ball falls to the left or to the right with the probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$. Each row is a stage.

INTERACTIVE · THE TREE DIAGRAM WORKSHOP

First set “with replacement”. Choose an event or tap the ends of paths: the probabilities are multiplied and added.

EXAMPLE 3 · THROWING TWICE

A dice is thrown twice. How likely are two sixes? How likely is exactly one six?

Stages: six with $\tfrac{1}{6}$, no six with $\tfrac{5}{6}$. Two sixes: $\tfrac{1}{6} \cdot \tfrac{1}{6} = \tfrac{1}{36}$.

Exactly one six: two paths, $\tfrac{1}{6} \cdot \tfrac{5}{6} + \tfrac{5}{6} \cdot \tfrac{1}{6} = \tfrac{10}{36} = \tfrac{5}{18}$.

$P(\text{two sixes}) = \tfrac{1}{36} \approx 2.8\%$, $\;P(\text{exactly one}) = \tfrac{5}{18} \approx 27.8\%$

EXAMPLE 4 · THE WHEEL OF FORTUNE

A wheel of fortune shows red with $\tfrac{1}{2}$, blue with $\tfrac{1}{3}$, yellow with $\tfrac{1}{6}$. It is spun twice. How likely is the same colour twice?

Three paths: $\tfrac{1}{2} \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{3} \cdot \tfrac{1}{3} + \tfrac{1}{6} \cdot \tfrac{1}{6} = \tfrac{9}{36} + \tfrac{4}{36} + \tfrac{1}{36} = \tfrac{14}{36}$

$P = \tfrac{7}{18} \approx 38.9\%$

EXERCISES

A coin is tossed three times. Draw the tree diagram. How likely is heads three times, how likely exactly twice heads?

8 equally likely paths. Heads three times: $\tfrac{1}{8}$. Exactly twice (HHT, HTH, THH): $\tfrac{3}{8}$.

An urn holds 4 red balls and 1 blue ball. Two balls are drawn with replacement. Work out $P(\text{both red})$, $P(\text{both blue})$ and $P(\text{different colours})$.

$\tfrac{16}{25}$, $\tfrac{1}{25}$ and $\tfrac{4}{25} + \tfrac{4}{25} = \tfrac{8}{25}$. Check: $16 + 1 + 8 = 25$.

At the shooting wall, Lea scores with every shot with the probability 0.3. She shoots twice. How likely does she score twice, how likely at least once?

Twice: $0.3 \cdot 0.3 = 0.09$. At least once: $0.09 + 0.21 + 0.21 = 0.51$.

A Galton board has 3 rows of nails and 4 slots below. How likely does a ball land in the slot on the far left, how likely in the second slot from the left?

Far left only via the path LLL: $\tfrac{1}{8}$. Second slot: right once, three paths (RLL, LRL, LLR): $\tfrac{3}{8}$.

On a wheel of fortune, the probability of red twice in two spins is to be 0.36. How big must the red share be? What angle does the red sector have?

$p \cdot p = 0.36$, so $p = 0.6$. Angle: $0.6 \cdot 360^\circ = 216^\circ$.

TEST YOURSELF!

How likely are two sixes in two throws?

$\tfrac{1}{6} \cdot \tfrac{1}{6} = \tfrac{1}{36}$

Urn with 3 red and 2 blue balls, twice with replacement. How likely are both red? Give a decimal.

$\tfrac{3}{5} \cdot \tfrac{3}{5} = \tfrac{9}{25} = 0.36$

A coin is tossed twice. How likely is heads exactly once?

$\tfrac{1}{4} + \tfrac{1}{4} = 0.5$

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Dependent or independent: with and without replacement

The bag holds 3 red and 2 blue balls. If the first red ball is not put back, there are only 2 red ones among 4 balls for the second draw. The probabilities of the second stage depend on the first draw.

KEY POINT · REPLACEMENT AND COMPLEMENTARY EVENT

With replacement: the same probabilities apply at every stage. The draws are independent of each other.

Without replacement: after each draw the number and the make-up change. The probabilities of the next stage depend on the result so far.

Complementary event: $P(\overline{E}) = 1 - P(E)$. Particularly handy for “at least once”: $P(\text{at least once}) = 1 - P(\text{never})$.

Without replacement are, for example, card games, the lottery and tickets from a bucket.

No memory: a dice does not know what came up before. Throws are always independent.

INTERACTIVE · WITHOUT REPLACEMENT

Compare the numbers on the branches of the second stage: without replacement and with replacement. Change the number of balls too.

EXAMPLE 5 · TWO RED BALLS

3 red and 2 blue balls, two are drawn without replacement. How likely are both red? Compare with replacement.

Without replacement: $\tfrac{3}{5} \cdot \tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{6}{20} = \tfrac{3}{10} = 0.3$. With replacement: $\tfrac{3}{5} \cdot \tfrac{3}{5} = \tfrac{9}{25} = 0.36$.

Without replacement, “both red” is less likely: 30% instead of 36%.

EXAMPLE 6 · AT LEAST ONE SIX

How likely is at least one six in four throws?

Complementary event: no six, $\left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^4 = \tfrac{625}{1296}$. So $1 - \tfrac{625}{1296} = \tfrac{671}{1296} \approx 0.518$.

A little more than 50%. Without the complementary event you would have to add 15 paths.

EXERCISES

A bag holds 2 red and 3 green balls. Two are drawn without replacement. Work out $P(\text{both red})$, $P(\text{both green})$ and $P(\text{different colours})$.

$\tfrac{2}{5} \cdot \tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{1}{10}$, $\;\tfrac{3}{5} \cdot \tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{3}{10}$, $\;1 - \tfrac{1}{10} - \tfrac{3}{10} = \tfrac{6}{10}$

Give the probability of the complementary event. a) throwing a six   b) drawing a winning ticket at a tombola with 20% winners   c) an event with $P(E) = 0.07$

a) $\tfrac{5}{6}$ (no six)   b) $0.8$ (a blank)   c) $0.93$

A bucket holds 4 winning tickets and 16 blanks. You draw two tickets. How likely are both wins? How likely is at least one win?

$\tfrac{4}{20} \cdot \tfrac{3}{19} = \tfrac{12}{380} \approx 0.032$. At least one win: $1 - \tfrac{16}{20} \cdot \tfrac{15}{19} = 1 - \tfrac{240}{380} = \tfrac{140}{380} \approx 0.368$.

How likely is at least one six in three throws?

$1 - \left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^3 = 1 - \tfrac{125}{216} = \tfrac{91}{216} \approx 0.421$

How many times must you throw at least, so that the probability of at least one six is over 90%? Try it out with the calculator.

We need $\left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^n < 0.1$. $\left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^{12} \approx 0.112$, $\left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^{13} \approx 0.093$. So at least 13 times.

TEST YOURSELF!

3 red and 2 blue balls, two without replacement. How likely are both blue?

$\tfrac{2}{5} \cdot \tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{1}{10}$

$P(E) = 0.35$. How big is the probability of the complementary event?

$1 - 0.35 = 0.65$

A coin is tossed three times. How likely is heads at least once?

$1 - \tfrac{1}{8} = \tfrac{7}{8} = 0.875$

UNIT 42 LESSONS

4Counting

A bicycle lock has three rings with the digits 0 to 9. For each digit on the first ring there are 10 on the second, for each of these pairs another 10 on the third. That makes $10 \cdot 10 \cdot 10 = 1000$ possibilities. Anyone who guesses has a chance of $\tfrac{1}{1000}$ at the first attempt.

KEY POINT · COUNTING PRINCIPLE AND FACTORIAL

Counting principle: if a choice has several steps with $n_1$, $n_2$, $n_3$, … possibilities, there are $n_1 \cdot n_2 \cdot n_3 \cdot \ldots$ possibilities in total.

Arrangements: $n$ different things can be arranged in $n! = n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot \ldots \cdot 2 \cdot 1$ ways, read “$n$ factorial”. For example $3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$.

If all the possibilities are equally likely, one particular one has the probability $\dfrac{1}{\text{number of possibilities}}$.

Calculator: the $x!$ key works out the factorial.

Factorials grow fast: $10! = 3{,}628{,}800$. That many seating orders already exist for ten people.

INTERACTIVE · ARRANGING AND COUNTING

Under “Arrangements” you see all the seating orders for up to four people. Under “Counting principle” you change the number of possibilities in each step.

EXAMPLE 7 · THE PIN

A PIN has four digits from 0 to 9. How many PINs are there? How likely is someone to guess it with three attempts?

$10 \cdot 10 \cdot 10 \cdot 10 = 10{,}000$. Three different attempts hit with the probability $\tfrac{3}{10{,}000} = 0.03\%$.

10,000 PINs, the chance of guessing is tiny.

EXAMPLE 8 · THE SEATING ORDER

Five people sit down at random on five chairs. How many seating orders are there? How likely are they to sit exactly in alphabetical order?

First chair 5 possibilities, second 4, then 3, 2, 1: $5! = 120$.

120 seating orders, the alphabetical one has the probability $\tfrac{1}{120}$.

EXERCISES

A canteen offers 3 starters, 4 main courses and 2 desserts. How many different menus with one of each course are there?

$3 \cdot 4 \cdot 2 = 24$

Work out $4!$, $6!$ and $7!$.

$24$, $720$, $5040$

Four runners reach the finish. How many orders are possible? How many possibilities are there just for gold and silver?

$4! = 24$ orders. Gold and silver: $4 \cdot 3 = 12$.

A suitcase lock has 4 rings with the digits 0 to 9. How long does it take at most to try all the combinations if one takes 2 seconds?

$10{,}000 \cdot 2\,\text{s} = 20{,}000\,\text{s} \approx 5.6$ hours.

A “word” is laid at random from the letters M, A, T, H, each letter exactly once. How many words are there? How likely does it begin with M? How likely is it MATH?

$4! = 24$ words. $3! = 6$ of them begin with M: $\tfrac{6}{24} = \tfrac{1}{4}$. MATH: $\tfrac{1}{24}$.

TEST YOURSELF!

Work out $5!$.

$5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 120$

How many outfits are there from 3 T-shirts and 2 pairs of trousers?

$3 \cdot 2 = 6$

A lock has 3 rings with 10 digits each. How likely are you to guess the combination at the first attempt?

$\tfrac{1}{1000} = 0.001$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Two dice are thrown. How likely is a total of 12, how likely a total of 7?

Total 12 only with 6 and 6: $\tfrac{1}{36}$. Total 7 with 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1: $\tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac{1}{6}$.

Connect with percentages: on two days it rains with a probability of 20% each, independently of each other. How likely do both days stay dry?

$0.8 \cdot 0.8 = 0.64 = 64\%$

A Galton board has 4 rows and 5 slots. How likely does a ball land on the far right? How likely in the middle (twice left, twice right)?

Far right: $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^4 = \tfrac{1}{16}$. Middle: 6 paths (LLRR, LRLR, LRRL, RLLR, RLRL, RRLL): $\tfrac{6}{16} = \tfrac{3}{8}$.

Three people meet. How likely do they all have their birthdays on different days? Calculate with 365 days.

The second person has a different day from the first with $\tfrac{364}{365}$, the third a different one from both with $\tfrac{363}{365}$: $\tfrac{364}{365} \cdot \tfrac{363}{365} \approx 0.992$.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

A bet from 1654

The French nobleman Chevalier de Méré liked to bet on dice. His first bet: in four throws at least one six comes up. He won with it in the long run, because the probability is $1 - \left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^4 \approx 51.8\%$.

His second bet: in 24 throws with two dice a double six comes up at least once. He thought this was just as favourable. But he lost in the long run: $1 - \left(\tfrac{35}{36}\right)^{24} \approx 49.1\%$. He asked the mathematician Blaise Pascal. In 1654 Pascal exchanged letters about it with Pierre de Fermat, and probability theory grew out of these letters.

Sources: correspondence between B. Pascal and P. de Fermat, summer 1654 (Œuvres de Fermat, volume 2). The numbers are recalculated with the complementary event.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

SIMULATION

a random device instead of the experiment, repeat very often; the relative frequency approximates the probability

94 sixes in 600 throws: 15.7%

PATH RULES

multiply along a path, add the paths of an event

exactly one six in two throws: $\tfrac{10}{36}$

REPLACEMENT · COMPLEMENTARY EVENT

without replacement the probabilities change; $P(\overline{E}) = 1 - P(E)$

$\tfrac{3}{5} \cdot \tfrac{2}{4} = 0.3$

COUNTING

multiply the numbers of the steps; arranging $n$ things: $n!$

lock: 1000, $5! = 120$

$\tfrac{2}{5} \cdot \tfrac{3}{4} + \tfrac{3}{5} \cdot \tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{6}{20} + \tfrac{6}{20} = 0.6$

$5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 60$
